q: Chandragupta I strengthened his position by marrying Kumaradevi, a princess of which clan?
explanation: Chandragupta I married the Licchavi princess Kumaradevi; their coins show both of them.

q: The poet Kalidasa is traditionally associated with the court of:
explanation: Kalidasa is counted among the Navaratnas (nine gems) of Chandragupta II Vikramaditya.

q: Which Gupta-age scholar stated that the Earth rotates on its axis?
explanation: Aryabhata, in his Aryabhatiya (499 CE), said the Earth rotates on its axis. India first satellite was named after him.

q: The rust-free Iron Pillar at Mehrauli (Delhi) is associated with a king named:
explanation: The Mehrauli pillar inscription names King Chandra, generally identified with Chandragupta II.

q: The gold coins issued by the Gupta rulers were called:
explanation: Gupta gold coins were called dinaras. Tanka and jital were Sultanate coins; karshapana was an older punch-marked coin.

q: Which Gupta ruler successfully repelled the invasion of the Hunas?
explanation: Skandagupta defeated the Hunas; this is recorded in his Bhitari pillar inscription.

q: Harshavardhana shifted his capital from Thanesar to:
explanation: Harsha moved his capital from Thanesar to Kannauj, which became the prize city of north India.

q: Harshavardhana was defeated on the banks of the Narmada by:
explanation: The Chalukya king Pulakeshin II stopped Harsha southward advance on the Narmada.

q: Which Sanskrit play was written by Harshavardhana himself?
explanation: Harsha wrote three plays: Nagananda, Ratnavali and Priyadarshika.

q: The rival powers in the "Tripartite Struggle" for control of Kannauj were:
explanation: From the 8th to 10th century the Palas of Bengal, Gurjara-Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas fought over Kannauj.

q: "Kavirajamarga", the earliest known work in Kannada, is attributed to:
explanation: Kavirajamarga is attributed to the Rashtrakuta king Amoghavarsha I (9th century).

q: The Pancha Rathas (five monolithic temples) at Mahabalipuram were built under:
explanation: The rathas were carved under the Pallava king Narasimhavarman I, called Mamalla; the town is named Mamallapuram after him.

q: Which Chola king took the title "Gangaikonda Chola" after his expedition to the Ganga?
explanation: Rajendra I led an army to the Ganga and built a new capital, Gangaikonda Cholapuram.

q: Which inscription gives details of village assemblies (sabha) under the Cholas?
explanation: The Uttaramerur inscriptions of Parantaka I describe election of village committees by lot.

q: The Sangam assemblies of Tamil poets were held under the patronage of which dynasty?
explanation: Tradition says three Sangams were held under the Pandya kings, the last at Madurai.

q: The Ajanta caves, famous for Buddhist paintings, are in which state?
explanation: Ajanta is in Aurangabad (Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar) district, Maharashtra; it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

q: The Great Stupa of Sanchi is located in which state?
explanation: The Sanchi Stupa, first built under Ashoka, stands near Vidisha in Madhya Pradesh.

q: The Ellora caves contain rock-cut shrines of which religions?
explanation: Ellora has 34 caves: Buddhist, Hindu and Jain, a symbol of religious harmony. Ajanta is only Buddhist.

q: Who wrote the Sanskrit grammar "Ashtadhyayi"?
explanation: Panini wrote the Ashtadhyayi, a grammar in eight chapters. Hook: Ashta = eight.

q: The ancient text "Sushruta Samhita" deals mainly with:
explanation: Sushruta is called the father of surgery; Charaka Samhita deals with general medicine.

q: Muhammad bin Qasim conquered Sindh in which year?
explanation: The Arab general Muhammad bin Qasim conquered Sindh in 712 CE, defeating Raja Dahir.

q: Mahmud of Ghazni plundered the Somnath temple in which year?
explanation: Mahmud raided Somnath in Gujarat in 1025 CE (attack completed early 1026), one of his 17 raids.

q: Al-Biruni, who came to India with Mahmud of Ghazni, wrote:
explanation: Al-Biruni wrote Kitab-ul-Hind (Tahqiq-i-Hind) in Arabic about Indian society and science. Rihla is by Ibn Battuta.

q: Who won the Second Battle of Tarain?
explanation: Muhammad Ghori defeated Prithviraj Chauhan in the Second Battle of Tarain, after losing the first one.

q: Qutb-ud-din Aibak died in 1210 at Lahore while:
explanation: Aibak fell from his horse while playing chaugan (polo) at Lahore in 1210.

q: Which Sultan introduced the silver "tanka" and copper "jital" coins?
explanation: Iltutmish standardised Sultanate currency with the silver tanka and copper jital.

q: The "Turkan-i-Chahalgani" (group of Forty nobles) was organised by:
explanation: Iltutmish created the Chahalgani; Balban later broke its power.

q: Which Sultan set up a separate military department, the "Diwan-i-Arz"?
explanation: Balban created the Diwan-i-Arz to reorganise the army against the Mongol threat.

q: Who founded the Khalji dynasty in 1290?
explanation: Jalal-ud-din Khalji founded the dynasty in 1290; his nephew Alauddin killed him and took the throne in 1296.

q: Which general led Alauddin Khalji campaigns into South India?
explanation: Malik Kafur led expeditions against Devagiri, Warangal, Dwarasamudra and Madurai.

q: The Alai Darwaza near the Qutub Minar was built by:
explanation: Alauddin Khalji built the Alai Darwaza (1311), the first building with a true arch and dome in India. Hook: Alai = Alauddin.

q: Muhammad bin Tughlaq shifted his capital from Delhi to:
explanation: In 1327 Muhammad bin Tughlaq moved the capital to Devagiri, renamed Daulatabad, then returned to Delhi.

q: Which Sultan brought two Ashokan pillars from Topra and Meerut to Delhi?
explanation: Firoz Shah Tughlaq moved the Topra and Meerut pillars to Delhi; one stands at Feroz Shah Kotla.

q: The "Diwan-i-Khairat", a department of charity, was set up by:
explanation: Firoz Shah Tughlaq created the Diwan-i-Khairat to help the poor, orphans and widows.

q: Timur invaded India in 1398 during the reign of:
explanation: Timur sacked Delhi in 1398 when the weak Tughlaq ruler Nasir-ud-din Mahmud was on the throne.

q: Who founded the Sayyid dynasty in 1414?
explanation: Khizr Khan, Timur governor of Multan, founded the Sayyid dynasty in 1414.

q: Who founded the Lodi dynasty?
explanation: Bahlul Lodi founded the Lodi dynasty in 1451, the first Afghan dynasty of Delhi.

q: The city of Agra was founded in 1504 by:
explanation: Sikandar Lodi founded Agra in 1504 and made it his capital; the Mughals later developed it.

q: Which poet is known as "Tuti-e-Hind" (Parrot of India)?
explanation: Amir Khusrau, court poet of the Khaljis, was called Tuti-e-Hind for his sweet poetry.

q: Babur wrote his memoirs, the Baburnama, in which language?
explanation: Babur wrote the Baburnama (Tuzuk-i-Baburi) in his mother tongue Turki; it was later translated into Persian under Akbar.

q: In which battle of 1540 did Sher Shah decisively defeat Humayun?
explanation: Sher Shah beat Humayun at Chausa (1539) and finally at Kannauj or Bilgram (1540), after which Humayun went into exile.

q: The tomb of Sher Shah Suri is located at:
explanation: Sher Shah tomb stands in the middle of a tank at Sasaram in Bihar, his birthplace.

q: In the Second Battle of Panipat, Akbar forces under Bairam Khan defeated:
explanation: Hemu, general of Adil Shah Sur, was defeated at Panipat in 1556.

q: Akbar promulgated the Din-i-Ilahi in:
explanation: Din-i-Ilahi (Tauhid-i-Ilahi) was announced in 1582. Birbal was among its few followers.

q: Akbar built the Ibadat Khana (House of Worship) for religious debates at Fatehpur Sikri in:
explanation: The Ibadat Khana was built in 1575; at first only Muslims debated there, later all faiths joined.

q: Akbar abolished the jizya tax in:
explanation: Akbar abolished the jizya in 1564; Aurangzeb reimposed it in 1679.

q: Aurangzeb reimposed the jizya in:
explanation: Aurangzeb reimposed the jizya on non-Muslims in 1679, reversing Akbar 1564 decision.

q: The Mansabdari system of ranking nobles and officers was introduced by:
explanation: Akbar introduced the Mansabdari system with ranks called zat and sawar.

q: Which Mughal emperor hung a "chain of justice" (Zanjir-i-Adl) so subjects could seek justice?
explanation: Jahangir hung a golden chain of justice at Agra Fort that anyone could pull to seek justice.

q: Who is regarded as the chief architect of the Taj Mahal?
explanation: Ustad Ahmad Lahori is generally credited as chief architect of the Taj Mahal, built by Shah Jahan for Mumtaz Mahal.

q: The famous Peacock Throne (Takht-i-Taus) was made for:
explanation: The Peacock Throne was made for Shah Jahan; Nadir Shah carried it away to Persia in 1739.

q: The Red Fort of Delhi was built by:
explanation: Shah Jahan built the Red Fort (completed 1648) in his new city Shahjahanabad.

q: The Bibi ka Maqbara, often called the "Taj of the Deccan", is in:
explanation: Bibi ka Maqbara at Aurangabad is the tomb of Aurangzeb wife Dilras Banu Begum, built by their son Azam Shah.

q: Dara Shikoh translated the Upanishads into Persian under the title:
explanation: Dara Shikoh translated 50 Upanishads as Sirr-i-Akbar (The Great Secret). Majma-ul-Bahrain was his own work. Razmnama is the Persian Mahabharata.

q: In the war of succession, Aurangzeb defeated Dara Shikoh at Samugarh in:
explanation: The Battle of Samugarh (1658) settled the war of succession; Aurangzeb then imprisoned Shah Jahan in Agra Fort.

q: Guru Nanak was born at:
explanation: Guru Nanak was born in 1469 at Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib in Pakistan.

q: The Adi Granth was compiled in 1604 by:
explanation: The fifth Guru, Arjan Dev, compiled the Adi Granth in 1604 and installed it in the Harmandir Sahib.

q: The Khalsa was founded in 1699 by:
explanation: Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur on Baisakhi day, 1699.

q: The Bhakti saint Mirabai was a devotee of:
explanation: Mirabai, a Rajput princess, composed bhajans to Krishna, whom she called Giridhar Gopal.

q: "Sursagar" is the famous work of which Bhakti poet?
explanation: Surdas, the blind poet of Braj, wrote Sursagar in praise of child Krishna. Hook: Sur-sagar = Surdas.

q: The Chishti Sufi order was established in India by:
explanation: Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti founded the Chishti order in India; his dargah is at Ajmer.

q: The Suhrawardi Sufi order in India was established by Bahauddin Zakariya at:
explanation: Bahauddin Zakariya established the Suhrawardi order at Multan; unlike the Chishtis, they accepted state grants.

q: Hampi, the capital of the Vijayanagara Empire, lies on the banks of which river?
explanation: Hampi (Vijayanagara) stands on the Tungabhadra in Karnataka and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

q: The "Ashtadiggajas", eight great Telugu poets, adorned the court of:
explanation: Krishnadeva Raya court had the Ashtadiggajas, including Allasani Peddana.

q: The Persian envoy Abdur Razzaq visited Vijayanagara during the reign of:
explanation: Abdur Razzaq, envoy of the Timurid ruler Shah Rukh, visited in 1443 under Deva Raya II.

q: The Portuguese traveller Domingo Paes visited Vijayanagara during the reign of:
explanation: Domingo Paes visited about 1520 and praised the grandeur of Krishnadeva Raya capital.

q: Mahmud Gawan, the famous Bahmani minister, built a great madrasa at:
explanation: Mahmud Gawan built the madrasa at Bidar, the later Bahmani capital, in 1472.

q: The Gol Gumbaz at Bijapur is the tomb of:
explanation: Gol Gumbaz, with one of the largest domes and a whispering gallery, is the tomb of Muhammad Adil Shah.

q: The Charminar at Hyderabad was built by:
explanation: Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah built the Charminar in 1591 when he founded Hyderabad.

q: In the Third Battle of Panipat, the Marathas were defeated by:
explanation: Ahmad Shah Abdali of Afghanistan defeated the Marathas under Sadashivrao Bhau at Panipat in 1761.

q: "Chauth", a tax collected by the Marathas, was what fraction of the land revenue?
explanation: Chauth was one-fourth (chau = four); Sardeshmukhi was an extra one-tenth.

q: The Treaty of Purandar (1665) was signed between Shivaji and:
explanation: Raja Jai Singh of Amber, sent by Aurangzeb, forced Shivaji to sign the Treaty of Purandar and give up 23 forts.

q: Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in:
explanation: Vasco da Gama landed at Calicut in May 1498, opening the sea route from Europe to India.

q: The Portuguese captured Goa in 1510 under:
explanation: Albuquerque took Goa from the Bijapur Sultan in 1510; it remained Portuguese until 1961.

q: The English East India Company received its charter in 1600 from:
explanation: Queen Elizabeth I granted the charter on 31 December 1600.

q: The island of Bombay came to the English Crown in 1661 as dowry of:
explanation: Portuguese princess Catherine of Braganza married Charles II; Bombay was part of her dowry. Charles leased it to the Company in 1668.

q: Pondicherry, the chief French settlement in India, was founded in 1674 by:
explanation: Francois Martin founded Pondicherry in 1674. Colbert set up the French East India Company (1664); Dupleix came later.

q: Who became the first Governor-General of Bengal under the Regulating Act of 1773?
explanation: Warren Hastings became the first Governor-General of Bengal (Fort William) in 1774.

q: The Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774) was set up under which Act?
explanation: The Regulating Act of 1773 provided for a Supreme Court at Calcutta, with Sir Elijah Impey as first Chief Justice.

q: The Board of Control to supervise the East India Company was created by:
explanation: Pitt India Act (1784) created the Board of Control, giving the British government a say in Indian affairs.

q: Which Act first set aside Rs 1 lakh a year for education in India?
explanation: The Charter Act of 1813 ended the Company trade monopoly (except tea and China trade) and set aside Rs 1 lakh for education.

q: Which Act introduced open competition for recruitment to the civil services?
explanation: The Charter Act of 1853 opened the civil services to competitive examination.

q: Which Act ended Company rule and transferred power to the British Crown?
explanation: After the 1857 revolt, the Government of India Act 1858 created the post of Secretary of State for India; the Governor-General became Viceroy.

q: Which Indian state was the first to accept Wellesley Subsidiary Alliance (1798)?
explanation: The Nizam of Hyderabad accepted the Subsidiary Alliance first, in 1798.

q: Tipu Sultan died in 1799 defending which place?
explanation: Tipu was killed defending his capital Srirangapatna in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War, 1799.

q: The Treaty of Amritsar (1809) was signed between the British and:
explanation: Through the Treaty of Amritsar, negotiated by Charles Metcalfe, Ranjit Singh accepted the Sutlej as his eastern boundary.

q: The Ryotwari system of land revenue is associated with:
explanation: Thomas Munro (with Alexander Read) introduced the Ryotwari system in Madras, settling revenue directly with the ryot (peasant).

q: The Mahalwari system of land revenue was introduced by:
explanation: Holt Mackenzie proposed the Mahalwari system (1822), settling revenue with the village (mahal) as a unit in north-west India.

q: Mangal Pandey attacked British officers on 29 March 1857 at:
explanation: Sepoy Mangal Pandey of the 34th Bengal Native Infantry revolted at Barrackpore near Calcutta.

q: Who was the Governor-General of India during the Revolt of 1857?
explanation: Lord Canning was Governor-General in 1857 and became the first Viceroy in 1858.

q: Who led the Revolt of 1857 at Kanpur?
explanation: Nana Saheb, adopted son of Peshwa Baji Rao II, led the rising at Kanpur.

q: After the Revolt of 1857, Bahadur Shah Zafar was exiled to:
explanation: The last Mughal emperor was exiled to Rangoon (Yangon), where he died in 1862.

q: Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi died fighting the British in 1858 near:
explanation: After losing Jhansi and Kalpi, Lakshmibai captured Gwalior and died fighting there in June 1858.

q: What was the real name of Tantia Tope?
explanation: Tantia Tope was born Ramachandra Pandurang (Tope); Dhondu Pant was the real name of Nana Saheb.

q: The Paika Rebellion of 1817 in Odisha was led by:
explanation: Bakshi Jagabandhu, military chief of the Raja of Khurda, led the Paika Rebellion in 1817.

q: The "Ulgulan" (Great Tumult) of 1899-1900 was led by:
explanation: Birsa Munda led the Munda Ulgulan in the Ranchi region; his birth anniversary, 15 November, is Janjatiya Gaurav Divas.

q: The Kuka (Namdhari) movement in Punjab was led by:
explanation: Baba Ram Singh led the Kuka movement; the British deported him to Rangoon.

q: The Moplah (Mappila) rebellion of 1921 took place in:
explanation: The Moplah uprising of 1921 occurred in the Malabar region of Kerala, during the Khilafat-Non-Cooperation period.

q: The Arya Samaj was founded in 1875 by:
explanation: Dayananda Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj at Bombay in 1875 with the call "Go back to the Vedas".

q: "Satyarth Prakash" was written by:
explanation: Satyarth Prakash (1875) is the main text of the Arya Samaj, written by Dayananda Saraswati.

q: The Ramakrishna Mission was founded in 1897 by:
explanation: Vivekananda founded the Ramakrishna Mission in 1897 in the name of his guru, with service to humanity as its aim.

q: The Theosophical Society set up its headquarters in India at:
explanation: Founded in New York (1875) by Blavatsky and Olcott, the Society moved its headquarters to Adyar near Madras in 1882.

q: The Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College at Aligarh (1875) was founded by:
explanation: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan founded the MAO College, which became Aligarh Muslim University in 1920.

q: The Self-Respect Movement (1925) in Tamil Nadu was started by:
explanation: Periyar E. V. Ramasamy launched the Self-Respect Movement against caste discrimination in 1925.

q: The SNDP Yogam (1903) in Kerala was founded under the inspiration of:
explanation: The Sree Narayana Dharma Paripalana Yogam was founded in 1903 to uplift the Ezhava community, inspired by Sree Narayana Guru.

q: The Servants of India Society (1905) was founded by:
explanation: Gokhale founded the Servants of India Society at Poona in 1905 to train selfless national workers.

q: Who is regarded as the founder of the Indian National Congress?
explanation: Allan Octavian Hume, a retired British civil servant, founded the Congress in 1885.

q: How many delegates attended the first session of the Indian National Congress in 1885?
explanation: 72 delegates met at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay, in December 1885.

q: Who was the first Muslim President of the Indian National Congress?
explanation: Badruddin Tyabji presided over the 1887 Madras session.

q: Who was the first Indian woman to be President of the Indian National Congress?
explanation: Sarojini Naidu presided over the 1925 Kanpur session. Annie Besant (1917) was the first woman president but not Indian-born.

q: The "Drain Theory", explained in "Poverty and Un-British Rule in India", was put forward by:
explanation: Dadabhai Naoroji, the "Grand Old Man of India", explained how wealth was drained from India to Britain.

q: At which Congress session (1906), presided by Dadabhai Naoroji, was "Swaraj" declared the goal?
explanation: At the 1906 Calcutta session, Naoroji declared Swaraj as the goal of the Congress.

q: The Lucknow Pact of 1916 was an agreement between:
explanation: In 1916 at Lucknow the Congress and the Muslim League agreed on joint demands; the Moderates and Extremists also reunited there.

q: Who gave the slogan "Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it"?
explanation: Tilak, called "Lokmanya", gave this slogan during the Home Rule movement.

q: Tilak founded his Home Rule League in April 1916 at:
explanation: Tilak League was set up at Belgaum in April 1916; Annie Besant started hers at Madras in September 1916.

q: Mahatma Gandhi returned to India from South Africa on:
explanation: Gandhi landed at Bombay on 9 January 1915; this day is celebrated as Pravasi Bharatiya Divas.

q: Whom did Mahatma Gandhi regard as his political guru?
explanation: Gandhi called Gokhale his political guru; on Gokhale advice he toured India for a year after returning.

q: The Kheda Satyagraha (1918) in Gujarat was against:
answer: Collection of land revenue despite crop failure
explanation: In Kheda, peasants refused to pay revenue after crop failure; Gandhi led them with Vallabhbhai Patel. (Indigo = Champaran, mill wages = Ahmedabad.)

q: Who ordered the firing at Jallianwala Bagh on 13 April 1919?
explanation: Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer ordered the firing; Michael O’Dwyer was the Lieutenant-Governor of Punjab.

q: Who renounced his knighthood in protest against the Jallianwala Bagh massacre?
explanation: Tagore returned his knighthood in 1919 in protest against the Amritsar massacre.

q: The British government committee that inquired into the Jallianwala Bagh massacre was headed by:
explanation: The Hunter Committee (Disorders Inquiry Committee, 1919) investigated the massacre.

q: The Khilafat Movement in India was led by:
answer: Ali Brothers (Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali)
explanation: The Ali Brothers led the Khilafat Movement in support of the Turkish Caliph; Gandhi joined it with Non-Cooperation.

q: Which leader died of injuries from a police lathi-charge during the protest against the Simon Commission at Lahore?
explanation: Lala Lajpat Rai, the "Punjab Kesari", died in November 1928 after the lathi-charge. The Simon Commission had no Indian member.

q: The Nehru Report (1928) was prepared by a committee headed by:
explanation: The Nehru Report, drafted by a committee under Motilal Nehru, asked for Dominion Status.

q: The "Fourteen Points" (1929) were put forward by:
explanation: Jinnah presented his Fourteen Points in 1929 in response to the Nehru Report.

q: Gandhi began the Dandi March on 12 March 1930 from:
explanation: Gandhi marched from Sabarmati Ashram (Ahmedabad) to Dandi and broke the salt law on 6 April 1930.

q: Mahatma Gandhi attended which Round Table Conference in London?
explanation: After the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931), Gandhi attended the Second Round Table Conference as the sole Congress representative.

q: The Poona Pact of 1932 was signed between Gandhi and:
explanation: The Poona Pact replaced separate electorates for Depressed Classes (Communal Award) with reserved seats in joint electorates.

q: The Karachi session of Congress (1931), which adopted the resolution on Fundamental Rights, was presided over by:
explanation: Sardar Patel presided at Karachi (1931), where resolutions on Fundamental Rights and economic policy were passed.

q: Provincial autonomy was introduced by which Act?
explanation: The 1935 Act ended dyarchy in the provinces and gave them autonomy; elections were held in 1937.

q: "Dyarchy" in the provinces was introduced by which Act?
explanation: The Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (Act of 1919) split provincial subjects into "reserved" and "transferred" lists: dyarchy.

q: At the Tripuri session (1939), Subhas Chandra Bose was re-elected Congress President defeating:
explanation: Bose defeated Gandhi candidate Pattabhi Sitaramayya in 1939 but soon resigned and formed the Forward Bloc.

q: The Forward Bloc was founded in 1939 by:
explanation: After resigning as Congress President, Bose formed the All India Forward Bloc in 1939.

q: The "August Offer" of 1940 was made by which Viceroy?
explanation: Lord Linlithgow made the August Offer in 1940 to win Indian support in World War II.

q: Who was chosen by Gandhi as the first Individual Satyagrahi in 1940?
explanation: Vinoba Bhave was the first Individual Satyagrahi (October 1940); Nehru was the second.

q: The Quit India resolution was passed on 8 August 1942 at:
explanation: The AICC passed the Quit India resolution at Gowalia Tank (now August Kranti Maidan), Bombay.

q: Which lawyer led the defence of INA officers in the Red Fort trials of 1945?
explanation: Bhulabhai Desai led the defence of Shah Nawaz Khan, P. K. Sahgal and G. S. Dhillon; Nehru also wore the barrister gown again.

q: The Royal Indian Navy mutiny of February 1946 began at:
explanation: Ratings of HMIS Talwar at Bombay began the RIN mutiny in February 1946; it spread to Karachi and other ports.

q: The Cabinet Mission of 1946 was headed by:
explanation: The mission had three members: Pethick-Lawrence (leader), Stafford Cripps and A. V. Alexander.

q: The Muslim League observed "Direct Action Day" on:
explanation: Direct Action Day (16 August 1946) led to the Great Calcutta Killings. 23 March 1940 was the Lahore (Pakistan) Resolution.

q: The plan for the partition of India was announced on 3 June 1947 by:
explanation: The Mountbatten Plan (3 June Plan) of 1947 provided for partition into India and Pakistan.

q: The boundary commissions that drew the India-Pakistan border in 1947 were chaired by:
explanation: The Radcliffe Line was drawn by Cyril Radcliffe. McMahon Line = India-China, Durand Line = Afghanistan-Pakistan.

q: Who was the first and only Indian Governor-General of independent India?
explanation: C. Rajagopalachari (Rajaji) succeeded Mountbatten in June 1948 and served until 26 January 1950.

q: Who is often called the "Father of Armed Rebellion" in India for his 1879 uprising in Maharashtra?
explanation: Vasudev Balwant Phadke organised an armed band against British rule in 1879; he died in prison at Aden.

q: In 1897 the Chapekar brothers assassinated which plague commissioner at Poona?
explanation: Damodar and Balkrishna Chapekar shot W. C. Rand for the harsh plague measures in Poona (1897).

q: The secret society "Abhinav Bharat" was founded by:
explanation: Vinayak Damodar Savarkar and his brother Ganesh founded Abhinav Bharat (1904) in Nasik.

q: India House in London, a centre for Indian revolutionaries, was founded by:
explanation: Shyamji Krishna Varma founded India House (1905) and the journal "The Indian Sociologist".

q: In 1909, Madan Lal Dhingra shot dead which British official in London?
explanation: Madan Lal Dhingra killed Sir William Curzon Wyllie in London in July 1909 and was hanged.

q: When the Komagata Maru returned to India in 1914, its passengers were fired upon at:
explanation: The ship, refused entry at Vancouver, came back to Budge Budge, where police fired on the passengers in September 1914.

q: The Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA) was formed in 1928 at:
explanation: Revolutionaries including Bhagat Singh and Chandrashekhar Azad renamed the HRA as HSRA at Feroz Shah Kotla in 1928.

q: In 1928, Bhagat Singh and Rajguru shot which police officer at Lahore, mistaking him for Scott?
explanation: To avenge Lala Lajpat Rai, they targeted SP James Scott but killed ASP J. P. Saunders (December 1928).

q: Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru were hanged on:
explanation: They were hanged in Lahore Jail on 23 March 1931; the day is observed as Shaheed Diwas.

q: Chandrashekhar Azad died in an encounter in 1931 at:
explanation: Azad died at Alfred Park, Allahabad on 27 February 1931; the park is now Chandrashekhar Azad Park.

q: In 1940, Udham Singh assassinated which British official in London?
explanation: Udham Singh shot Michael O’Dwyer, Punjab Lieutenant-Governor at the time of Jallianwala Bagh, in March 1940.

q: The Chittagong Armoury Raid of 1930 was led by:
explanation: "Masterda" Surya Sen led the raid on 18 April 1930 with the Indian Republican Army.

q: The Vernacular Press Act (1878) was passed during the viceroyalty of:
explanation: Lord Lytton gagged Indian-language newspapers by the Vernacular Press Act; Lord Ripon repealed it in 1882.

q: Which Viceroy is called the "Father of Local Self-Government" in India?
explanation: Lord Ripon resolution of 1882 laid the foundation of local self-government.
